### Why healthcare services

**GRANT:** Why does healthcare get its own episode?

**MAYA:** Because it combines the two things we said matter most in episode one. A shortage of skilled people, and a huge amount of repetitive judgment work around them. And it's a big part of private equity portfolios: physician practice platforms, home health and hospice, behavioral health, dental and veterinary groups, physical therapy, labs, ambulatory surgery centers, and the tech-enabled services companies that support them with billing, staffing and data.

**GRANT:** And the margins are thin.

**MAYA:** Very. AlixPartners published an analysis last November on AI in healthcare private equity. Their figures for the prior three years had healthcare providers growing revenue around nine and a half percent with margins under two percent, and HealthTech with faster growth but EBITDA margins under three percent. When margins are that thin, a few points of labor efficiency changes the whole return.

**GRANT:** And labor is most of the cost.

**MAYA:** In most provider businesses, labor is the largest cost by far, and it's the cost that's been rising fastest. Clinical salaries, agency staffing to cover vacancies, and the administrative staff who handle scheduling, intake, billing and insurance. And the administrative side is unusually large in US healthcare, because of the complexity of getting paid.

**GRANT:** So the opportunity is on both sides. Give clinicians time back, and reduce the administrative load.

**MAYA:** And there's a third one that's specific to healthcare. Revenue integrity. Getting paid correctly for work you've already done. Denied claims, under-coded visits, missing documentation and prior authorization delays are all leakage, which is the first lever from episode one. In a business with a two percent margin, recovering one percent of revenue that was leaking is a fifty percent increase in profit.

**GRANT:** Say that again.

**MAYA:** If your margin is two percent and you recover one percent of revenue, your profit goes from two to three. That's fifty percent more. That's why revenue cycle AI gets so much attention from healthcare investors.

---

### The scribe evidence, in depth

**GRANT:** Let's start with the most visible AI tool in healthcare. The ambient scribe.

**MAYA:** The ambient scribe listens to the visit, with the patient's consent, and drafts the clinical note: the history, the exam findings, the assessment and the plan. The clinician reviews it, edits it and signs it. Adoption has been extraordinarily fast. Health systems, physician groups and now smaller practices have rolled them out, and several big electronic health record vendors have built their own.

**GRANT:** And physicians are using AI more generally.

**MAYA:** They are. The American Medical Association surveys physicians on this, and its survey published in early 2025 found that about two thirds of physicians reported using some form of AI in their practice in 2024, up from about thirty eight percent the year before. Documentation was one of the most common uses.

**GRANT:** So what does the best evidence say about whether scribes actually work?

**MAYA:** We mentioned it in episode one, but it deserves a proper look. In April, JAMA published a study led by Mass General Brigham and UCSF. It followed more than eighteen hundred clinicians using AI scribes across five hospitals for over two years, and compared them with more than six thousand seven hundred clinicians who weren't using them.

**GRANT:** That's a big, long study.

**MAYA:** It's the kind of evidence we rarely get for business tools. And the results were real but modest. The scribes cut documentation time by about sixteen minutes a day, around ten percent. Clinicians saw about half an extra patient visit a week. The revenue effect was statistically significant but small, around a hundred and sixty seven dollars a month per clinician.

**GRANT:** So if a scribe costs more than that per month, it doesn't pay for itself on revenue alone.

**MAYA:** On revenue alone, in that study, at average usage, it might not. Which is why the more interesting part of the study is the variation. Clinicians who used the scribe for more than half of their visits saw about three times the documentation reduction. But only about a third of users got to that level.

**GRANT:** So the tool worked for the people who used it a lot.

**MAYA:** And most people didn't use it a lot. That's the adoption lesson again. And it changes how an operator should think about a scribe rollout. The question isn't "does the scribe work?" It's "how do we get more clinicians to use it on most of their visits, and what do we do with the time it frees?"

**GRANT:** What stops clinicians from using it more?

**MAYA:** The reasons you hear are practical. The note style doesn't match how they like to write. It takes longer to edit a long AI draft than to write a short note themselves. Some visit types, like quick follow-ups or procedures, don't benefit much. Some patients decline. Some clinicians worry about errors creeping into the record, like the AI attributing a symptom to the wrong side of the body or mishearing a medication name.

**GRANT:** Those errors are a real concern.

**MAYA:** They are, and the clinician signing the note is accountable for every word in it. So training matters. Clinicians need to know where these tools tend to make mistakes and read those parts carefully. And practices should audit a sample of AI-drafted notes, comparing them with what happened in the visit, at least in the first months.

**GRANT:** And the value beyond revenue?

**MAYA:** That's where the case gets stronger. Clinician burnout and retention. If a scribe is part of why a physician stays, rather than moving to a competitor or retiring early, the value of that is large, because replacing a physician is expensive and slow. Many health systems justify scribes on retention and satisfaction, and some of the published studies have shown improvements in clinicians' reported burnout and cognitive load. For a private equity platform that depends on recruiting and keeping clinicians, that's a real lever. It's just harder to put in a spreadsheet.

**GRANT:** So how would you write the business case?

**MAYA:** Honestly. A modest direct time saving, with a range that depends on adoption. A destination for the time, agreed with clinical leaders: more visits, shorter days, or both. A retention assumption, stated separately so the board can judge it. And a measurement plan: notes completed same day, after-hours charting time, visits per clinician day, clinician satisfaction, and turnover. Then manage adoption actively, because that's where the value is decided.

---

### Where else AI is working

**GRANT:** Where else is AI actually working?

**MAYA:** Documentation beyond the visit. AlixPartners described one client that cut after-call work by more than half in a care-management setting, which let clinicians see more patients. That's their client example, so it's one data point, but it matches what you hear across the sector. Call summaries, care plans, referral letters, discharge instructions and prior authorization letters are all documentation, and all good candidates.

**GRANT:** What else?

**MAYA:** Self-service for routine questions. The same analysis described a virtual assistant that handled questions about benefits, copays and coverage, and said that in one deployment more than seventy percent of activated members used it for most simple interactions. That frees the human advocates for the hard cases.

**GRANT:** And on the patient access side? Scheduling, intake, the phone?

**MAYA:** Everything we said in episode two about the phone applies to healthcare, with extra care. Practices miss calls too, and a missed call from a new patient is a lost patient. AI can answer, schedule, reschedule, check insurance eligibility, send intake forms and answer basic questions about directions and preparation. The rule is that it must recognize anything clinical, like chest pain or a medication question, and hand it to a person or direct the patient to emergency care immediately.

**GRANT:** And on the clinical-adjacent side?

**MAYA:** Targeted outreach. Models that combine claims, clinical and engagement data to flag people at risk, so a care team can call them before they end up in hospital. In value-based care, where the provider takes financial risk for a population, that's directly a margin lever. Closing care gaps, like overdue screenings, also affects quality scores, which affect payment.

**GRANT:** And in clinical research?

**MAYA:** Clinical research services, like contract research organizations, are documentation-heavy and highly regulated. Permira described AI in adverse event case processing, which is the work of handling reports of side effects in drug trials and after approval. They said it cut intake time by a quarter while improving auditability.

**GRANT:** I notice every example has a human checking the output.

**MAYA:** That's not an accident. In regulated work, the value comes from AI doing the first draft and a qualified person signing off. The draft might be ninety percent right, but the person is still accountable for the other ten. If you design a workflow where nobody is clearly accountable for the final output, you've designed a compliance problem.

---

### The patient front door

**GRANT:** Let's spend a bit more time on the front door, because in a lot of practices that's where patients decide whether to stay.

**MAYA:** It's the phone, the online booking page, the portal and the intake forms. And in many practices it's under real strain. Front desk staff answer phones while checking patients in, verify insurance while someone is waiting, and chase missing referrals between calls. Hold times get long, calls get abandoned, and new patients book elsewhere.

**GRANT:** So what does a good AI front door look like?

**MAYA:** A patient can call at any hour and book, reschedule or cancel a routine appointment with an AI assistant that's connected to the real schedule and knows the practice's rules, like which visit types need a referral or which provider sees which conditions. Insurance eligibility is checked automatically before the visit, and the patient is told in advance if there's a problem, rather than at the desk. Intake forms are sent by text, filled in on the phone, and checked for missing information. And reminders go out with an easy way to reschedule, which cuts no-shows.

**GRANT:** And the hard part?

**MAYA:** Knowing what not to handle. Anything clinical goes to a nurse or the emergency protocol. Anything about a bill dispute, a complaint or a sensitive result goes to a person. And the assistant should never give medical advice, even when the patient asks a simple question like whether they can take ibuprofen before their procedure. That's for a clinician.

**GRANT:** How would you measure it?

**MAYA:** Call abandonment rate, time to next available appointment for new patients, no-show rate, share of visits with insurance verified in advance, and front desk overtime. And patient satisfaction, specifically about access. In many practices, fixing the front door does more for patient experience than anything clinical, because it's where most frustration happens.

**GRANT:** And what about the time AI gives back to the front desk?

**MAYA:** Same rule as everywhere: decide its destination. In many practices, the best use is calling patients who need to be scheduled, like people overdue for follow-up or who didn't book their next visit, and helping patients with financial questions before the visit. That turns time saved into visits and collections, rather than letting it disappear.

---

### Value-based care

**GRANT:** You mentioned value-based care. For people who don't live in healthcare, explain why AI looks different there.

**MAYA:** In traditional fee-for-service, a provider is paid for each visit, test or procedure. In value-based care, the provider takes responsibility for the total cost and quality of care for a group of patients, and shares in the savings, or the losses. Medicare Advantage, accountable care organizations and many primary care platforms that private equity has backed work this way.

**GRANT:** So the incentives flip.

**MAYA:** They flip. Under fee-for-service, AI value is mostly about doing more visits more efficiently and getting paid correctly for them. Under value-based care, a large part of the value is preventing expensive events. An avoided hospital admission, an emergency visit that turned into a phone call with a nurse, a diabetic patient whose blood sugar was controlled before it caused a complication. Those are worth thousands of dollars each.

**GRANT:** And AI helps how?

**MAYA:** Three ways. Finding the patients who need attention, by combining claims, clinical records, pharmacy data and sometimes social factors like transport or housing, so a care team calls the right people first. Making each care manager more productive, with call summaries, care plan drafts and task lists, so they can handle more patients well. And documentation accuracy, because in Medicare Advantage, payment is risk adjusted, meaning it depends on how sick the patients are, as documented.

**GRANT:** And risk adjustment is another bright line.

**MAYA:** One of the brightest. Risk adjustment coding has been a major enforcement focus, with large government settlements over diagnoses that weren't supported by the record. AI that helps find diagnoses which are real, documented and being treated is legitimate. AI that mines old records for diagnoses to add to claims without a current clinical basis is exactly what regulators have been pursuing. Same rule as coding: accuracy, an accountable clinician, and audits.

**GRANT:** How would you measure outreach AI?

**MAYA:** Against a comparison group. If the model flags a thousand high-risk patients and the care team calls them, you want to know whether their admissions fell compared with similar patients who weren't called, or who were called later. Without a comparison, every outreach program looks like it works, because high-risk patients tend to look better over time anyway. Statisticians call it regression to the mean. Operators call it a board slide that falls apart in diligence.

---

### The revenue cycle

**GRANT:** We can't talk about healthcare services without talking about getting paid.

**MAYA:** No. The revenue cycle is the full journey from scheduling a patient to collecting the last dollar. Eligibility checks, prior authorization, documentation, coding, claim submission, denial management, appeals, patient billing and collections. Every step can leak money, and every step is full of AI opportunity.

**GRANT:** Take me through the big ones.

**MAYA:** Coding first. After a visit, someone has to translate the documentation into billing codes. AI can suggest codes from the note, flag where the documentation doesn't support the code, and catch missing elements that would support a more accurate code. Then claim scrubbing: checking each claim against the payer's rules before it's sent, so it isn't rejected for a missing modifier or an eligibility problem. Then denial prediction: flagging claims likely to be denied, so someone fixes them first.

**GRANT:** And when claims are denied?

**MAYA:** Appeals. A lot of denied claims are never appealed, because appeals take time and the staff are busy. But a meaningful share of appeals succeed. AI can draft appeal letters from the record and the payer's policy, so a person can review and send many more of them. That's straightforward revenue recovery.

**GRANT:** And prior authorization.

**MAYA:** Prior authorization is where a lot of the pain is. Before certain services, the provider needs the insurer's approval. Staff spend hours on portals, faxes and phone calls, and delays mean patients wait for care. AI can gather the clinical information, fill in the request, track its status and draft responses to requests for more information.

**GRANT:** And the rules on prior authorization changed recently.

**MAYA:** They did, which is good news for providers. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services finalized an interoperability and prior authorization rule in early 2024. For Medicare Advantage plans, Medicaid and some others, it required payers, starting in January 2026, to decide on standard requests within seven calendar days and urgent ones within seventy two hours, to give a specific reason for denials, and to publicly report prior authorization metrics. And by January 2027, those payers have to support electronic prior authorization through standard interfaces.

**GRANT:** So the plumbing is getting better.

**MAYA:** Slowly, but yes. And that matters for AI, because AI works best when it can connect to a standard electronic interface rather than a fax machine. A provider business that invests in electronic prior authorization now will get more value from automation as the payers' side catches up.

**GRANT:** And the payers are using AI too.

**MAYA:** They are, which makes this something of an arms race. Payers use algorithms to review claims and authorizations, and that's been controversial. There have been lawsuits, filed in 2023 and since, alleging that some insurers used algorithms to deny care inappropriately in Medicare Advantage. Those cases are about payer practices, and they're still in the courts. And CMS itself started a model this year called WISeR, testing AI-assisted prior authorization review for a set of services in traditional Medicare in six states.

**GRANT:** So providers face AI on the other side of the table.

**MAYA:** Increasingly. Which is one more reason providers need good documentation and good tools of their own. When the payer's system reads your documentation, it had better be complete and accurate.

---

### The bright line

**GRANT:** But there's a line here.

**MAYA:** A bright one. Coding has to reflect what actually happened. An AI tuned to maximize reimbursement is a compliance risk, and potentially a False Claims Act risk, which in the US means treble damages and penalties per claim. Upcoding has been an enforcement priority for years, and the government has its own analytics to spot unusual coding patterns.

**GRANT:** So what's the right goal for coding AI?

**MAYA:** Accuracy. Catch the under-coding, because under-coding is real and common, and catch the missing documentation, so clinicians can document what they actually did. But never invent anything, and never nudge the documentation toward a higher code that isn't supported. If the AI suggests a code, the documentation has to support it, and a qualified coder or clinician has to own the decision.

**GRANT:** How do you make that real, not just a policy?

**MAYA:** Four controls. Your compliance team owns the rules the AI follows, not the vendor and not the revenue team. Someone audits a sample of AI-assisted coding every month, against the documentation, and tracks the error rate in both directions. You watch your coding distribution over time, because if the share of high-level visits jumps after an AI rollout, you need to be able to explain why with evidence. And you document all of it, because if a payer or a regulator asks, you'll want to show the controls existed before they asked.

**GRANT:** And the vendor contract?

**MAYA:** Read what the vendor promises and what they don't. Some revenue cycle vendors are paid a share of the revenue they recover. That can align incentives nicely, or it can create pressure toward aggressive coding. Know which you have, and make sure your own compliance controls don't depend on the vendor's incentives.

---

### Specialties in the portfolio

**GRANT:** Let's go through some of the specialties that show up in private equity portfolios. Dental first.

**MAYA:** Dental service organizations are one of the classic healthcare roll-ups. AI shows up in three places. Imaging, where FDA-cleared tools flag possible findings on dental X-rays, like decay or bone loss, which helps the dentist explain the treatment plan to the patient and supports the claim. Front office, with scheduling, recall reminders, insurance verification and phones. And revenue cycle, especially attaching the right documentation to claims.

**GRANT:** There's a concern with imaging AI, though.

**MAYA:** The same bright line. An imaging tool that flags possible decay is a second pair of eyes. It shouldn't become a reason to recommend more treatment than the dentist would otherwise recommend. A platform should watch treatment rates by location and dentist before and after, for the same reason a physician group watches its coding distribution.

**GRANT:** Veterinary.

**MAYA:** Veterinary groups are a similar roll-up story, with less regulation on the billing side, because most clients pay directly. Scribes for veterinary visits are growing fast. Client communication is a big one: reminders for vaccines and checkups, follow-ups after procedures, and answering the flood of calls. And the labor shortage among veterinarians and technicians makes time-saving tools a recruiting argument.

**GRANT:** Home health and hospice.

**MAYA:** Home health is a scheduling and documentation business delivered in patients' homes. Matching clinicians to visits by location, skills and patient preference looks a lot like field service dispatch. Documentation is heavy, because Medicare's home health assessments are long and drive payment. AI can help clinicians document at the point of care, by voice, and check the assessment for consistency. The same accuracy rule applies, because the assessment drives the payment.

**GRANT:** And behavioral health.

**MAYA:** Behavioral health has a severe shortage of clinicians and long waitlists, so time savings matter a lot. Scribes for therapy sessions exist and are popular with some clinicians. But this is the most sensitive data in healthcare. Some substance use disorder treatment records have special federal protections beyond normal health privacy rules, under what's called Part 2, and those rules were updated in 2024 with a compliance date in February 2026. Patients may be more reluctant to have sessions recorded. So consent has to be genuine, the clinician has to be comfortable, and the vendor's data handling has to be excellent.

**GRANT:** And labs and diagnostics?

**MAYA:** Labs are high-volume, process-driven businesses where AI helps with order intake, billing and quality control, and in some cases image analysis in pathology. Many AI tools that analyze medical images are regulated as medical devices. The FDA has authorized more than a thousand AI-enabled devices, mostly in radiology. If a portfolio company builds or changes a tool that makes clinical findings, that's a regulatory question, not just a product one.

---

### Choosing healthcare AI vendors

**GRANT:** How should a healthcare platform choose among the vendors? There are a lot of scribe and revenue cycle companies now.

**MAYA:** There are, and the market is consolidating, which is itself a risk. I'd ask six questions. First, integration: does it write directly into our electronic health record and practice management system, in the right fields, or does someone copy and paste? Copy and paste is where errors and wasted time come from.

**GRANT:** Second.

**MAYA:** Specialty fit. A scribe built for primary care may produce poor notes for physical therapy, behavioral health or dentistry. Ask to test it on your own visit types, with your own clinicians, and compare the notes. Third, the agreements: a business associate agreement, clear terms on data retention, whether recordings are kept and for how long, and whether your data trains their models.

**GRANT:** Fourth.

**MAYA:** Evidence. Ask what they've measured with customers like you, and how. Time saved per day, by how many clinicians, over what period. If the evidence is a survey of satisfied users, that's useful but it's not the same as measured time. Fifth, controls: can your compliance team see and set the rules, especially for coding? Can you audit what the tool suggested and what the human accepted?

**GRANT:** And sixth.

**MAYA:** Price and exit. Per clinician per month, per encounter, or a share of recovered revenue. Model all of them at your real volumes. And ask what happens if the vendor is acquired, which in this market is quite likely. Make sure your data comes back to you in a usable form.

---

### The US rulebook

**GRANT:** Let's do regulation, because there's a lot of it.

**MAYA:** In the US, the baseline is unchanged. Patient data is protected health information under HIPAA, so any AI vendor touching it needs a business associate agreement. You need to know where the data goes, how long it's kept, whether it's used to train the vendor's models, and who at the vendor can see it. And the minimum necessary rule still applies, so don't send a tool more patient data than it needs.

**GRANT:** What about staff using general chat assistants?

**MAYA:** That's the most common real-world HIPAA risk with AI right now. A busy staff member pastes a patient's details into a consumer chatbot to draft a letter. If there's no business associate agreement with that provider, that's a potential breach. The fix is the same as in episode one: give staff an approved tool with the right agreement in place, and a short, clear policy.

**GRANT:** And beyond HIPAA?

**MAYA:** A few things worth knowing. The federal nondiscrimination rule under Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act now says that covered healthcare organizations must make reasonable efforts to identify and reduce the risk of discrimination from patient care decision support tools, including AI, with that requirement in effect since May 2025. So if you use a tool that helps decide who gets outreach, which patients are high risk, or who gets scheduled first, you should know what inputs it uses and check whether it treats groups differently.

**GRANT:** And the states.

**MAYA:** The states are active. California, for example, requires providers that use generative AI to write patient communications about clinical information to disclose that, unless a licensed provider reviewed the message. California also passed a law saying that decisions to deny or change care based on medical necessity in utilization review must be made by a licensed clinician, not by an algorithm alone. Several other states have similar bills or laws. And then there's the broader set of state rules on automated decision-making. Foley's piece mentioned California, Colorado and New York, covering decisions like hiring, pricing, credit and insurance.

**GRANT:** That's a lot to keep track of.

**MAYA:** It is, and it changes every legislative session. That's why we made a whole separate show about it, The Rulebook. For an operator, the practical approach is to keep an inventory of every AI tool, what it decides or drafts, and where a person reviews it. If you have that inventory, a new state law becomes a checklist exercise instead of a fire drill.

---

### Europe

**GRANT:** And Europe, for funds with European portfolio companies?

**MAYA:** The EU AI Act timeline moved. In May, the EU institutions agreed the Digital Omnibus on AI, which pushed back the high-risk obligations. For stand-alone high-risk systems listed in Annex III, things like recruitment and credit scoring tools, the date moved from August 2026 to December 2027. For AI embedded in regulated products, like medical devices, it moved to August 2028.

**GRANT:** So companies got a reprieve.

**MAYA:** On the high-risk rules, yes. But the transparency obligations in Article 50 still applied from August 2026, with a short grace period for some watermarking requirements. That includes telling people when they're interacting with an AI system, which matters for patient-facing chat and phone tools. And the general-purpose model rules have applied since August 2025, though those mostly land on the model providers.

**GRANT:** What would you tell a European healthcare services company?

**MAYA:** Use the extra time to build the documentation and risk management you'll need anyway, rather than to stop. And remember that the AI Act sits on top of the GDPR, which already treats health data as a special category with strict rules, and on top of the medical device regulations. In Europe, the data protection work is usually the bigger near-term job.

---

### Beyond healthcare

**GRANT:** You said "other regulated work." What else fits this pattern?

**MAYA:** Anything where the paperwork is the product. Insurance claims administration, where third-party administrators handle claims for insurers and employers. Inspection and testing, like environmental or safety testing labs. Compliance services, like the background check and workforce compliance world. Clinical research services. Accounting and tax services, which private equity has been buying actively. And parts of financial services, like loan servicing.

**GRANT:** Pick one and walk through it.

**MAYA:** Insurance claims administration. A claim arrives with documents: forms, photos, medical records, invoices. Someone has to read it, check coverage, check for fraud signals, decide what to pay or what to investigate, and write it all up. AI can classify and extract from the documents, summarize the file, flag inconsistencies and draft the decision letter. An adjuster makes the decision. The cycle time drops, and adjusters handle more claims. And because insurance decisions are one of the areas covered by state automated decision-making rules and insurance regulators' own guidance on AI, the controls need to be documented.

**GRANT:** And accounting firms?

**MAYA:** Accounting is a big one this year, because private equity has been buying accounting firms at a fast pace. The work is documentation-heavy and seasonal, with a shortage of accountants. AI helps with data gathering from clients, document review, drafting workpapers and tax returns for review, and answering client questions. But it runs straight into the business services pricing question from episode two. If a firm bills by the hour and AI halves the hours on routine returns, it has to change how it prices. And for audit work, the independence and professional standards rules apply on top.

**GRANT:** And the common rules across all of these?

**MAYA:** The same rules apply: AI drafts, an accountable person signs, every output can be traced back to its sources, and the compliance team owns the guardrails. If you can say those four things about every AI workflow in a regulated business, you're in good shape.

**GRANT:** And a buyer at exit will check all of that.

**MAYA:** They will. And increasingly, so will the insurers. The Foley piece noted that representations and warranties insurers are starting to exclude AI-specific risks. If you can show clean controls, you're in a better position than a company that can't.

### Harbor Therapy: sizing it

**GRANT:** Let's do the math for a made-up company. Harbor Therapy, an outpatient physical therapy platform with sixty clinics and three hundred therapists.

**MAYA:** Start with documentation. Suppose each therapist spends about ninety minutes a day on notes, and much of that happens after hours. A scribe or voice documentation tool that saves even fifteen minutes a day, at realistic adoption, gives back about seventy five hours of therapist time per day across the platform. If a visit is forty five minutes, and half of the saved time goes to more visits, that's around fifty more visits a day. At, say, a hundred dollars per visit, that's about five thousand dollars a day, or more than a million dollars a year.

**GRANT:** And if therapists use the time to go home earlier instead?

**MAYA:** Then you don't get the revenue, but you may get lower turnover. Physical therapy has high turnover in some markets. If better tools reduce turnover by a few points, the savings on recruiting, onboarding and lost productivity can be similar in size. That's why you decide the destination of the time with the clinical leaders in advance, and measure it.

**GRANT:** And the revenue cycle?

**MAYA:** Suppose Harbor's denial rate is eight percent, and about half of denied claims are never worked. AI-assisted claim checking before submission might cut avoidable denials, and AI-drafted appeals let the billing team work all of them instead of half. If Harbor bills a hundred million a year, even recovering half a percent of revenue is half a million dollars, at very high margin. Plus a reduction in days in accounts receivable.

**GRANT:** And the front desk?

**MAYA:** Missed calls and no-shows. Physical therapy depends on patients completing their full course of visits, and dropouts are lost revenue and worse outcomes. Automated reminders, easy rescheduling by text or AI phone, and outreach to patients who fall off their plan are all simple and measurable. Track the visits completed per plan of care.

**GRANT:** So three workflows, three ranges.

**MAYA:** And each one with an owner. The clinical director for documentation. The revenue cycle director for denials. The operations director for scheduling and retention. Same pattern as every other sector.

---

### What goes wrong in healthcare AI

**GRANT:** Let's do failure modes, healthcare edition.

**MAYA:** Five. The first is the confident error. A scribe that mishears a drug name, puts a finding on the wrong side, or records something the patient didn't say. Most of these are caught when the clinician reviews the note. The risk is when review becomes a quick glance because the drafts are usually right. The fix is training, sampling audits, and making it easy to edit.

**GRANT:** Second.

**MAYA:** The automation that nobody owns. A tool that sends patients reminders or answers portal messages, set up by a vendor, configured once, and never reviewed again. Then a payer changes a rule, or a clinic changes its hours, and the tool keeps giving out the old information. Every patient-facing automation needs a named owner and a regular review.

**GRANT:** Third.

**MAYA:** Alert fatigue. Risk models and decision support tools that fire too many alerts get ignored, which is worse than no alerts, because now the organization thinks it has a safety net and it doesn't. Fewer, better alerts, tuned with the clinicians who receive them.

**GRANT:** Fourth.

**MAYA:** Vendor concentration and cyber risk. Healthcare learned this painfully in February 2024, when a ransomware attack on Change Healthcare, a major claims processing company, disrupted payments for providers across the country for weeks, and eventually affected the data of an enormous number of people. That wasn't an AI failure, but it's the lesson for AI. Every new vendor that touches patient data or the payment flow is a new dependency and a new attack surface. Ask about security, ask about their own vendors, and have a plan for what you'd do if they went down for a month.

**GRANT:** And fifth.

**MAYA:** The quiet drift into aggressive. Nobody decides to upcode. But a coding tool suggests the higher code when the documentation is borderline, coders accept suggestions because it's faster, the numbers improve, and a year later the coding distribution is an outlier compared with peers. That's why we keep saying: watch the distribution, audit samples, and let compliance own the rules.

---

### Questions we keep hearing

**GRANT:** A few quick questions from healthcare operators. Should we let the electronic health record vendor's AI do everything?

**MAYA:** It's often the right starting point, because it's already integrated and covered by your existing agreements. But compare it honestly with specialist tools on the workflows that matter most to you, and don't assume the bundled option is cheaper once it's priced separately at renewal.

**GRANT:** Will payers pay less if we're more efficient?

**MAYA:** Not directly in fee-for-service, because rates aren't set on your cost. In value-based contracts, efficiency is the point. Where it matters is in negotiations with payers who see you using AI to recover more revenue. Be ready to show that your coding is more accurate, not more aggressive.

**GRANT:** How do we handle a clinician who refuses to use the tools?

**MAYA:** Don't force it, at least at first. Make the tools available, show results from peers, and fix the workflow problems they raise. Many skeptics become advocates when the note templates match how they work. Some never will, and for experienced clinicians who are productive without it, that's fine.

**GRANT:** And our biggest risk?

**MAYA:** Patient trust. Every AI decision in healthcare touches someone who is sick, worried, or both. If you keep that in mind, most of the other answers follow.

---

### A playbook for regulated work

**GRANT:** Give me the playbook.

**MAYA:** Six steps. One, start with documentation and administrative work, not clinical decisions. Two, keep a qualified human signing every output that goes to a patient, a payer or a regulator. Three, sign proper agreements with every vendor, and know where your data goes. Four, measure time saved, adoption, error rates, denial rates and audit findings, not just usage. Five, watch the distributions, like coding levels and treatment rates, so you can prove the AI made you more accurate, not more aggressive. And six, write down your controls now, because your next buyer, your insurer and possibly a regulator will ask for them.

**GRANT:** And the people side?

**MAYA:** Involve clinicians from day one. If the tool saves them an hour a day and they helped choose it, they'll champion it. If it's imposed and gets things wrong in front of patients, it's dead within a month. Let them try two or three options, let them shape the note templates, and give them a fast way to report problems. And remember the scribe study: the value sits with the clinicians who use it on most visits, so put effort into helping the occasional users become regular ones.

**GRANT:** And patients?

**MAYA:** Tell patients what's happening and ask for consent where it's needed, especially for recording. Most patients are comfortable when it's explained simply, like "this tool helps me take notes so I can look at you instead of my screen." That sentence, by the way, is one of the best arguments for the technology. When it works, the clinician pays attention to the patient again.
